title: 10. Simulated wildfire smoke exposure impairs growth performance of beef heifers.
content:
Abstract
Although the evidence of wildfire smoke effects on livestock is emerging, research remains limited, with most studies relying on uncontrolled natural exposure conditions that are difficult to predict and reproduce. To address this knowledge gap, our team has developed a controlled environment to investigate the responses of beef heifers exposed to controlled smoke mimicking natural wildfire smoke conditions. A two-year study was conducted, where 16 recently weaned heifers (Angus × Hereford; 8 months, 230 ±12 kg) were housed in individual pens in an enclosed barn for 36 days. The study was divided into 3 phases: baseline (d-7 to d0), where heifers were acclimated to the environment; smoke exposure (d1 to d7), where heifers were exposed to controlled, simulated wildfire smoke daily for 7 consecutive days; and post-smoke exposure (d8 to d28), where heifers were monitored for 3 weeks following smoke exposure. Smoke was produced every afternoon for 7 consecutive days to reduce air quality and mimic wildfire conditions. Air quality was monitored daily with two air quality monitors using PM2.5 as the primary criterion. Heifers were individually fed alfalfa hay ad libitum with intake recorded daily. Body weights (BW) were recorded weekly, along with collection of blood samples to evaluate physiological markers. Preliminary data were analyzed over time using the MIXED procedure of SAS, with each heifer as its own control and year included as a random effect. Air quality, measured with PM2.5, varied significantly over time (P ≤ 0.0001), reaching a daily average of 142 mg/m3 during smoke exposure, substantially exceeding the EPA 24-h air quality standard for humans (35 mg/m3). As expected, growing heifers gained weight over the duration of the study (P < 0.001), with BW increasing from 230 to 252 ± 12 kg. However, no changes in BW were detected between sampling days corresponding to the smoke exposure (d0 to 7; P ≥ 0.29) and the subsequent post-smoke exposure week (d7 to 14; P ≥ 0.32). Average daily gain (ADG) changed over time (P = 0.024), exhibiting positive ADG during the baseline phase (0.98 ± 0.22 kg/d), but declining during the smoke exposure (0.75 ± 0.22 kg/d), and becoming negligible in the two weeks post-smoke exposure (P ≤ 0.01; 0.10 ± 0.22, and −0.07 ± 0.33 kg/d, respectively for d7 to d14 and d14 to d21). From d21 to d28, ADG partially recovered (0.37 ± 0.33 kg/d) and did not differ from the baseline (P = 0.13). These findings indicate that wildfire smoke exposure negatively affects growth performance of beef heifers and highlight the value of controlled research models for understanding and mitigating climate-driven stressors in livestock production systems.
